reasons: Contains weak development defaults for storage and the JWT secret, and nothing in this file stops them reaching production.
REDIS_URL is read by the code but is missing here.
Two settings describe the access token lifetime and it is not clear which one is used.
No automated check confirms that the production values were replaced.

terms.meaning: A named setting that the operating system or a file hands to a program when it starts.
A signed login token that proves who a user is when they make a request.
Multi-factor authentication, a second check such as a code from a phone app, in addition to a password.
Time-based one-time password, the six-digit code that changes every 30 seconds.
Browser rules that decide which websites are allowed to call the API.
The standard method for sending email through a mail server.
A temporary web link that lets someone upload or download one file without logging in to the app.
Key management service, a cloud service that stores and manages encryption keys.
A fast in-memory data store used here for short-lived data and background job queues.
A standard encryption method that protects stored secrets.

sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Core app, login, and Redis settings
sections.what: Groups the core settings: run mode, port, log level, allowed websites, the database address, login token lifetimes, lockout limits, the MFA encryption key, and Redis connection details. Most values are examples to replace.
sections.why: Likely reason: a single list of settings keeps local and production setup consistent. The security note in the file explains why the placeholder secrets must be replaced.
sections.watch_out: The JWT secret and the MFA encryption key must be replaced with strong random values, and the MFA key must differ from the JWT secret.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Storage, AI services, and email settings
sections.what: Covers file storage (S3 or MinIO), how long upload and download links stay valid, the 10 MB upload size cap, the addresses of the AI and OCR services, and the email server details.
sections.why: Likely reason: these settings point the API at outside services, and the defaults target a local development setup.
sections.watch_out: The storage login is a development default, and the email username and password are left empty, so email will not send until they are filled in.

summary: A template listing every setting the API reads, with example values, that a developer copies into a real local settings file.
purpose: Shows which settings exist, what each one controls, and which placeholder values must be replaced before real use.
why: Lets a new developer set up the API without reading all the code. The security comments warn that production secrets must be strong and random.
how: 1) Copy this file to a local settings file such as .env. 2) Replace the placeholder secrets, especially the JWT secret and the MFA encryption key. 3) Point the database, Redis, file storage, AI service, OCR service and email settings at real services. 4) Start the API, which reads these values at startup.
inputs: Values typed in by the developer. This file does not read anything itself.
outputs: Nothing directly. It is documentation for settings the app reads when it starts.
risks: The file storage login and the JWT secret are weak example values. If they reach production unchanged, someone who knows them could forge login tokens or reach stored files. The code reads REDIS_URL, but this file does not list it. JWT_ACCESS_EXPIRY and JWT_ACCESS_EXPIRY_SECONDS both describe the access token lifetime. Which one the code uses is not visible in this file.
debug: If the API will not start or cannot connect to a service, check that the value is set in a file the app loads (.env.local or .env). If a setting seems to have no effect, find the code that reads it, because this file enforces nothing. If login tokens behave oddly, compare the two access token lifetime settings.
